props.title: Bed and Board

sections.content: **Bed and Board** (1970) marks François Truffaut's fourth installment following Antoine Doinel, with Jean-Pierre Léaud delivering his most mature performance yet as the now-married protagonist. Following **The 400 Blows** (1959), **Antoine and Colette** (1962), and **Stolen Kisses** (1968), this entry captures Antoine's struggle with domestic life alongside Christine (Claude Jade). Truffaut masterfully balances comedy and melancholy, showing Antoine's job dyeing flowers and his eventual affair with a Japanese woman, all while maintaining the character's trademark mix of charm and immaturity.

sections.content: The film sits perfectly within the later French New Wave period, when directors like Truffaut were moving from their experimental roots toward more structured narrative storytelling. Compare this to Godard's **A Married Woman** (1964) or Rohmer's **My Night at Maud's** (1969) - all examining marriage and fidelity through distinctly French lenses. Truffaut's approach remains more accessible, mixing autobiography with fiction in ways that influenced later personal filmmakers like Woody Allen.

What makes **Bed and Board** (1970) particularly fascinating is its exploration of everyday married life, something rarely depicted with such honesty in cinema of the period. The film's intimate portrayal of domestic spaces and routines recalls **A Man and a Woman** (1966) while predicting later relationship studies like **Scenes from a Marriage** (1973). Antoine's courtyard apartment becomes a microcosm of Parisian life, populated by eccentric neighbors who provide both comedy and commentary. SUBHEAD: Evolution of the French New Wave

sections.content: By 1970, the French New Wave had matured beyond its initial revolutionary phase. **Bed and Board** represents this evolution perfectly - maintaining the movement's interest in character psychology and social observation while adopting a more classical shooting style. The handheld cameras and jump cuts of earlier New Wave films give way to more measured compositions, though Truffaut never loses his light touch or ability to capture spontaneous moments.
